section_summary: This section contains correspondence, memoranda, telegrams, and cross-reference sheets (1930–1936) regarding persistent proposals by United Press journalist Henry F. Misselwitz to organize professional baseball in Japan and inaugurate an international World Series between American and Japanese champions. Misselwitz repeatedly lobbied Secretaries of State Henry L. Stimson and Cordell Hull, as well as White House Assistant Secretary Stephen T. Early, seeking official or informal administration endorsement to aid his promotional efforts and foster Japanese-American goodwill. The Department of State consistently declined to provide official backing or authorize the public use of officials' names, maintaining an established policy against connecting the government with private commercial enterprises while affirming informal sympathy for athletic exchanges.

subfiles.about: A personal letter from Henry F. Misselwitz congratulating Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson on the London Naval Conference and requesting a weekend meeting in Washington.
subfiles.summary: Henry F. Misselwitz of the United Press Associations writes to Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson from New York planning a weekend visit to Washington and asking to meet. He sends regards to Mrs. Stimson and congratulates the Secretary on his work at the London Naval Conference, which Misselwitz followed closely via United Press cables. He requests a reply by wire or letter to confirm an appointment.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry F. Misselwitz to Henry L. Stimson

subfiles.about: A letter from Secretary Stimson regretting that he cannot meet with Misselwitz due to the visit of the President-elect of Brazil.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson replies to Henry F. Misselwitz's letter of June 4, expressing willingness to see him but stating it will be impossible over the coming two weekends. Stimson explains that his schedule is completely occupied with official duties surrounding the visit of Júlio Prestes, the President-elect of Brazil. He suggests that Misselwitz postpone his visit to Washington until after the Brazilian visit.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry L. Stimson to Henry F. Misselwitz

subfiles.about: A letter from Misselwitz agreeing to postpone his Washington visit and requesting a luncheon appointment on June 21.
subfiles.summary: Henry F. Misselwitz thanks Secretary Stimson for his letter of June 6 and acknowledges the demands of the visit of Brazilian President-elect Júlio Prestes. Misselwitz states that he has postponed his trip to Washington to the following weekend and asks whether a definite luncheon appointment can be scheduled for Saturday, June 21, 1930.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry F. Misselwitz to Henry L. Stimson

subfiles.about: A letter from Secretary Stimson explaining that he will be out of town on June 21 and offering only a brief midweek appointment.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson informs Henry F. Misselwitz that he will be away from Washington on Saturday, June 21, making a weekend appointment impossible. Stimson explains that overwhelming post-London Conference work has forced him to limit definite engagements severely. He notes that if Misselwitz visits during the middle of the week, he will attempt to see him briefly at his office.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry L. Stimson to Henry F. Misselwitz

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum analyzing Henry F. Misselwitz's proposal to organize baseball in Japan and establish a World Series.
subfiles.summary: Ransford S. Miller of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs summarizes Henry F. Misselwitz's proposal to organize baseball in Japan, establish an international World Series, and serve as the American advisor to promote mutual understanding. Miller notes Misselwitz's insistence that the project rely exclusively on Japanese capital and remain non-commercialized. However, Miller doubts that professional baseball could be established without commercialization or that Japanese capital is currently available, concluding that international sport fellowship must continue to rely on collegiate baseball exchanges.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Ransford S. Miller on Misselwitz's Proposal to Organize Baseball in Japan

subfiles.about: An archival document withdrawal sheet inserted into the file jacket.
subfiles.summary: This page is an archival document withdrawal sheet inserted into the State Department decimal file jacket. The text is faint and largely unreadable due to low OCR confidence, exhibiting fragments characteristic of archival withdrawal records. No substantive information about the removed or transferred item can be determined from the legible text.
subfiles.title: Document Withdrawal Sheet

subfiles.about: A memorandum forwarding Henry F. Misselwitz's letter to Dr. Hornbeck for advice and a draft reply.
subfiles.summary: An official in the Secretary's office (initialed E.R.M.) transmits Henry F. Misselwitz's incoming letter to Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs. The note observes that Misselwitz is a good friend of Secretary Stimson, who has not yet seen the proposal. Dr. Hornbeck is requested to submit a memorandum or draft reply setting forth his opinion to assist in responding.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from E. R. M. to Stanley K. Hornbeck

subfiles.about: A confidential letter proposing the organization of professional baseball in Japan and an international World Series to foster friendship.
subfiles.summary: Henry F. Misselwitz of the United Press Associations writes confidentially to Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson proposing the organization of professional baseball in Japan and the creation of an international World Series. Misselwitz emphasizes baseball's immense popularity in Japan, citing 75,000 spectators at high school championships and the sport's collegiate roots under Dr. Isoo Abe. He requests Stimson's confidential advice and unofficial support to keep the venture on a high plane, hoping to act as the American advisor and secure future personal economic independence while benefiting Japanese-American relations.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry F. Misselwitz to Henry L. Stimson

subfiles.about: A letter from Secretary Stimson expressing sympathy with the goal of international sports friendship but questioning the practicability of commercial baseball in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson replies confidentially to Henry F. Misselwitz's letter of October 2. Stimson states that he is in hearty sympathy with promoting good relations between Japan and the United States, but cannot share Misselwitz's optimism regarding the plan's feasibility. He questions how baseball could be organized without placing it on a commercial basis and doubts sufficient Japanese capital is available, suggesting Misselwitz test the concept informally with Japanese friends.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry L. Stimson to Henry F. Misselwitz

subfiles.about: A telegram thanking Secretary Stimson for his letter and requesting an appointment in Washington on Saturday.
subfiles.summary: Henry F. Misselwitz sends a telegram to Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson expressing high appreciation for his letter. Misselwitz states that he is arranging to travel to Washington on Saturday morning specifically to see the Secretary, and asks to be advised if a meeting would be convenient.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Henry F. Misselwitz to Henry L. Stimson

subfiles.about: A telegraphic reply from Secretary Stimson declining a weekend meeting due to his absence from Washington.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson responds by telegram to Henry F. Misselwitz's meeting request. Stimson informs Misselwitz that he will be leaving Washington on Friday noon and will be away until Monday afternoon, preventing any Saturday meeting.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Henry L. Stimson to Henry F. Misselwitz

subfiles.about: A letter outlining a detailed plan to seek support from organized baseball and requesting State Department letters of endorsement and introduction.
subfiles.summary: Henry F. Misselwitz follows up on his Japanese baseball proposal, asking Secretary Stimson for an informal letter expressing favor for the project and a letter of introduction to American Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes in Tokyo. Misselwitz argues that sound business methods are merely the necessary structure to support a noble ideal of Pacific understanding. He plans to approach Baseball Commissioner Kenesaw Mountain Landis and Chicago Cubs owner William Wrigley Jr. to sponsor the project and accompany him to Japan to consult with Japanese leaders.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry F. Misselwitz to Henry L. Stimson

subfiles.about: A letter declining official support for commercialized sports promotion but providing a general letter of introduction to diplomatic officers.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson replies to Henry F. Misselwitz's letter of October 15, reiterating sympathy for fostering friendly relations with Japan. However, Stimson firmly declines to lend official support to any particular plan designed to achieve this through commercialized enterprise, stating it must proceed through private channels. He encloses a general letter of introduction to American diplomatic and consular officers that Misselwitz may present to Ambassador Forbes in Tokyo or other representatives.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry L. Stimson to Henry F. Misselwitz

subfiles.about: A letter reporting progress with baseball authorities and inquiring whether Stimson's letter may be used in press announcements in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Henry F. Misselwitz informs Secretary Stimson that he discussed the Japanese baseball project with Baseball Commissioner Kenesaw Mountain Landis and league presidents John Heydler and E. S. Barnard, who are submitting the proposal to individual club owners. He also notes that major league baseball approved a tour of American players to Japan for the following autumn. Misselwitz inquires whether he is permitted to use Stimson's October 18, 1930 letter in personal and press statements upon arriving in Japan.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry F. Misselwitz to Henry L. Stimson

subfiles.about: A letter prohibiting the public or press use of Department correspondence in connection with a private enterprise.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson answers Henry F. Misselwitz's letter of January 7, explicitly requesting that Misselwitz not use the Secretary's letter of October 18, 1930 in making public or press announcements in Japan. Stimson explains that permitting the use of official correspondence in connection with a private enterprise violates a well-established Department policy based on sound, practical reasons. He concludes by congratulating Misselwitz on his progress and wishing him ultimate success.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry L. Stimson to Henry F. Misselwitz

subfiles.about: A telegram inquiring whether Secretary Stimson had received his letter of January 7.
subfiles.summary: Henry F. Misselwitz sends a brief telegram to Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson inquiring whether the Secretary had received his earlier letter dated January 7, 1931.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Henry F. Misselwitz to Henry L. Stimson

subfiles.about: A telegraphic reply confirming that Misselwitz's letter was received and a response mailed.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson sends a brief telegram to Henry F. Misselwitz in New York confirming that his letter was received and that an official written reply was mailed to him that day.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Henry L. Stimson to Henry F. Misselwitz

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet recording an invitation for the Harvard University baseball team to play in Japan.
subfiles.summary: This State Department document file note cross-references a letter dated December 27, 1933, from the President of Harvard University, filed under decimal file 032 Harvard Ball Team/1. The document concerns a proposed visit of the Harvard University baseball team to Japan and encloses an invitation for the team to compete against leading Japanese universities.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Visit of Harvard University Ball Team to Japan

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet recording an inquiry regarding Harvard baseball games in Japan.
subfiles.summary: This State Department document file note cross-references a telegram dated May 18, 1934, from Harvard athletic director William J. Bingham, filed under decimal file 032 Harvard Ball Team/3. The telegram advises of an invitation for the Harvard baseball team to play matches against Japanese universities and asks whether the games are being organized under the auspices of Japanese colleges.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Harvard Baseball Team Tour in Japan

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum advising against supporting a professional baseball league in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs analyzes Henry F. Misselwitz's renewed request for a letter from the Secretary of State or Ambassador Grew supporting a national major baseball league in Japan. The memorandum recommends against encouragement, noting that Japan has shown little real interest in professional baseball as opposed to collegiate games. Furthermore, it observes that past international baseball games between American and Japanese teams frequently harmed relations due to aggressive play and differing rule interpretations.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by the Division of Far Eastern Affairs on Proposed Professional Baseball League in Japan

subfiles.about: A letter asking for an informal letter from Secretary Hull or an introduction to Ambassador Grew for his baseball venture.
subfiles.summary: Henry F. Misselwitz writes to Michael J. McDermott, Chief of the Division of Current Information, in response to McDermott's communication regarding Misselwitz's letter to Stephen Early. Misselwitz states that while formal government action is inappropriate, an informal note of interest from Secretary Cordell Hull or an introduction to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew would be invaluable. He mentions his prior correspondence with Secretary Stimson, emphasizes the enduring Japanese enthusiasm for baseball, and asks that the matter be kept strictly confidential to prevent others from appropriating his idea.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry F. Misselwitz to Michael J. McDermott

subfiles.about: A letter enclosing Misselwitz's reply to McDermott and requesting that President Roosevelt be informed of the baseball project.
subfiles.summary: Henry F. Misselwitz writes to White House Assistant Secretary Stephen T. Early enclosing a copy of his reply to Michael J. McDermott. Misselwitz hopes that an informal note from the State Department can be obtained to help him enlist Judge Landis and organized baseball while keeping the government formally uncommitted. He asks Early to inform President Roosevelt of the project if appropriate and offers to discuss the idea in person.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry F. Misselwitz to Stephen T. Early

subfiles.about: A White House letter referring Henry F. Misselwitz's baseball proposal to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Stephen T. Early, Assistant Secretary to President Roosevelt, transmits a confidential letter received from Henry F. Misselwitz of the United Press to Michael J. McDermott at the State Department. Early describes Misselwitz's project to organize baseball in Japan as unique and interesting, but notes that there is no place for White House action. He requests that McDermott or someone else in the Department reply confidentially to Misselwitz explaining the positions of both the White House and State Department.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stephen T. Early to Michael J. McDermott

subfiles.about: A detailed proposal to the White House advocating the organization of the National League of Japan to improve diplomatic relations.
subfiles.summary: Henry F. Misselwitz writes a comprehensive confidential letter to White House Assistant Secretary Stephen T. Early proposing the establishment of the National League of Japan. Misselwitz argues that baseball can act as an effective 'New Deal' diplomatic tool to bring the American and Japanese peoples closer together and eventually lead to an international World Series. He cites the passion of Japanese fans, Babe Ruth's popularity, high school tournaments, and collegiate matches, and asks for informal administration encouragement and diplomatic introductions to help him organize the venture.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry F. Misselwitz to Stephen T. Early

subfiles.about: A memorandum recommending an informal White House reply to Misselwitz and enclosing a draft letter.
subfiles.summary: Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, advises Michael J. McDermott that Stephen T. Early should reply directly to Henry F. Misselwitz to maintain confidentiality and avoid formal departmental involvement. Hornbeck encloses a draft reply for Early stating that neither the White House nor the State Department can give official approval or backing to a private undertaking. The draft notes, however, that American officials abroad such as Ambassador Joseph C. Grew will continue appropriate informal courtesies, such as throwing out the first ball at athletic events.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Michael J. McDermott with Enclosed Draft Letter to Henry F. Misselwitz

subfiles.about: A letter informing Misselwitz that the administration cannot officially endorse a private commercial enterprise.
subfiles.summary: Michael J. McDermott, Chief of the Division of Current Information, writes to Henry F. Misselwitz on behalf of Stephen Early following consultations within the State Department. McDermott explains that the administration cannot provide official approval or backing for Misselwitz's Japanese baseball scheme, as associating with private undertakings would lead to endless similar demands and charges of discrimination. However, he assures Misselwitz that officials will watch the private effort with sympathetic interest and notes that Ambassador Joseph C. Grew and other diplomats will continue appropriate informal courtesies like throwing the ceremonial first pitch.
subfiles.title: Letter from Michael J. McDermott to Henry F. Misselwitz

subfiles.about: A memorandum providing a suggested draft reply to Misselwitz regarding a proposed letter of introduction.
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs submits to Michael J. McDermott a draft reply to Henry F. Misselwitz's letter of September 21, 1934. FE notes that issuing a letter of introduction without a congressional request should be cleared with the Secretary's office and the Passport Division. The enclosed draft letter reaffirms that the government cannot associate itself with a private commercial venture, but offers to arrange a general letter of introduction to American diplomatic officers abroad and transmit the recent correspondence to Ambassador Grew in Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from the Division of Far Eastern Affairs to Michael J. McDermott with Enclosed Draft Reply to Henry F. Misselwitz

subfiles.about: A letter following up on an in-person meeting with Secretary Hull regarding the National League of Japan, enclosing a suggested endorsement letter.
subfiles.summary: Henry F. Misselwitz writes to Secretary of State Cordell Hull following a personal conference in Hull's office regarding the establishment of the National League of Japan. Misselwitz claims that President Roosevelt and Japanese Ambassador Hirosi Saito privately expressed enthusiastic support for the initiative and envisioned an international World Series with games in New York, Washington, Japan, and Honolulu. He requests an informal expression of sympathy from Hull to help him obtain written backing from Commissioner Kenesaw Mountain Landis, enclosing a pre-drafted letter of endorsement for the Secretary's signature.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry F. Misselwitz to Cordell Hull with Enclosed Suggested Reply

subfiles.about: A letter on behalf of Secretary Hull declining to authorize the use of the Secretary's name in support of a private enterprise.
subfiles.summary: Harry A. McBride, Assistant to Secretary of State Cordell Hull, acknowledges receipt of Henry F. Misselwitz's letter of July 7, 1936. McBride states that after careful consideration, Secretary Hull finds no reason to alter the views expressed by former Secretary Stimson in 1931 and Michael J. McDermott in 1934. While wishing Misselwitz success, the Secretary does not feel warranted in authorizing the use of his name in support of a private commercial enterprise.
subfiles.title: Letter from Harry A. McBride to Henry F. Misselwitz

subfiles.about: A letter expressing regret over Secretary Hull's decision while thanking the Department for its informal interest.
subfiles.summary: Henry F. Misselwitz writes to Harry A. McBride acknowledging the Department's letter of July 11 regarding his efforts to organize the National League of Japan. Misselwitz expresses keen regret that Secretary Hull, like Secretary Stimson before him, views the project merely as a private enterprise rather than a powerful harbinger of Pacific peace and goodwill. Nevertheless, he expresses gratitude for the Secretary's personal interest and off-the-record good wishes.
subfiles.title: Letter from Henry F. Misselwitz to Harry A. McBride
